requirements.requirement: node2's inventory application log messages are forwarded to a centralized log collector on node1
requirements.summary: No pre-existing 'inventory' application was found on node2 (cmd-5b78e3d7d0b64894), so the executor created one (inventory-agent.sh + inventory.service, logger -t inventory -p local0.info) and configured rsyslog omfwd forwarding over TCP/601 to node1 with a disk-assisted queue. node1's imtcp listener on 601/tcp was verified active and forwarded messages were directly observed arriving and being filtered by fromhost-ip/programname.

requirements.requirement: Received messages are persisted on node1 at /var/log/inventory/node2.log
requirements.summary: Direct read of /var/log/inventory/node2.log on node1 shows live inventory log lines from node2 with correct ownership/permissions, and the file continued accumulating lines across the observation window (3 lines then 9 then 13).

requirements.requirement: Log flow continues working after either node1 or node2 restarts
requirements.summary: Executor captured healthy pre-restart baselines on both nodes (boot_id, active services, log tail), rebooted node1 first and directly observed the boot-id change (98aa35f5->7cd65f56) after connection loss/recovery, then verified rsyslog auto-started, listening on 601/tcp, and new/queued inventory log lines from node2 continued arriving in the destination file. It then rebooted node2, observed its boot-id change (6bb7e004->e07de7ab), verified rsyslog and inventory.service auto-started and re-established the TCP forwarding connection, and confirmed new post-restart entries landed in node1's log file. This is a direct, evidenced disruption-and-recovery transition for both nodes, not just static persistence config.

overall_summary: All three material outcomes of the task are satisfied with direct evidence: node2 runs a newly created 'inventory' application whose messages are reliably forwarded via rsyslog omfwd/imtcp to node1, persisted at /var/log/inventory/node2.log, and the flow was proven to survive both a node1 restart (with queued messages delivered afterward) and a subsequent node2 restart, each backed by pre-restart baseline, boot-id change, and post-restart recovery evidence. Hygiene is clean aside from a trivial, expected /tmp/reboot.log artifact per node from the intentional reboot commands.
limitations: The two restarts were performed sequentially (node1 then node2) rather than testing a simultaneous or overlapping-outage scenario; this is a reasonable and sufficient interpretation of 'after either system restarts' but does not cover a compound failure case.
No long-term persistence check beyond the immediate post-reboot window was captured (e.g., a second restart cycle), though systemd enablement was verified on both nodes.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands (rsyslog config creation on both nodes, firewall port opening on node1, inventory app/service creation on node2, deliberate reboots) trace directly to the material task outcomes or the required restart-recovery evidence protocol; no experimental or abandoned mutations were found. The only residue is a small /tmp/reboot.log left on each node from the backgrounded 'nohup sh -c reboot' scheduling commands (cmd-ef0d1841d62b474b, cmd-7a06d7b16d754672) — a low-risk, expected artifact of the intentional restart process, not troubleshooting debris. Package health checks and failed-service listings remain clean before and after. Firewall exposure was scoped to the necessary 601/tcp port with permanent+reload semantics rather than a temporary/broad rule.
